faq.q: Can gout be diagnosed without joint aspiration?

faq.a: Colchicine is cleared renally; accumulation can cause severe toxicity, so dose reduction or alternative therapy is needed.
faq.q: Why avoid colchicine in renal failure?

exam: A 48‑year‑old farmer presents with 2‑day sudden severe pain in the right first MTP joint, no fever. What is your immediate management and why? — Give NSAID trial, consider colchicine if NSAID contraindicated; explain need to rule out infection before steroids.
How would you differentiate acute gout from septic arthritis in a diabetic patient with a hot, swollen first MTP joint? — Discuss history, fever, leukocytosis, CRP, joint aspiration findings.

Explain the pathophysiological reason why lower temperature in distal joints favours crystal deposition. — Describe reduced solubility of urate at cooler temperatures leading to supersaturation and nucleation.

A patient with known chronic gout presents with a new first MTP swelling but normal serum uric acid. How do you interpret this? — Normal uric acid does not exclude gout; acute attacks can transiently lower levels; rely on clinical and crystal analysis.
What are the contraindications to using NSAIDs in acute podagra in a low‑resource setting? — Renal insufficiency, active peptic ulcer, uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure.

List three lifestyle measures that reduce recurrent gout attacks and explain the mechanism for each. — Reduce purine intake (less urate production), limit alcohol (decreases urate excretion), increase hydration (dilutes serum urate).
When is surgical intervention indicated for first MTP pathology? — Chronic tophaceous gout causing deformity, joint destruction, or refractory infection requiring debridement.
A patient on allopurinol develops an acute flare. What is the appropriate response? — Continue allopurinol, treat flare with NSAID/colchicine, educate that flares can occur during dose titration.
ai.title: First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint is the classic site for acute crystal arthropathies, especially gout, and for osteoarthritis in low‑resource settings. Recognising clinical patterns, using limited investigations and initiating appropriate therapy are essential for ward‑round competence.

b: Sudden onset of severe pain, swelling and erythema at the base of the big toe
Warmth and limited range of motion
History of hyperuricaemia, diuretic use, alcohol intake or rapid weight loss
sections.p: Podagra is an acute mono‑articular inflammation of the first MTP joint, most often caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition. Diagnosis rests on clinical presentation and, when possible, joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle‑shaped crystals.

t.b: Does the joint contain urate crystals? Positive finding confirms gout; absence suggests other causes.
Is hyperuricaemia present? Elevated level supports gout but normal level does not exclude it.
Are there erosions with overhanging edges? Suggests chronic gout; may also show osteoarthritis changes.

b: Mild: pain tolerable, able to ambulate with support
Moderate: pain limits walking, requires analgesia
Severe: incapacitating pain, fever, systemic inflammation
sections.p: Acute gout attacks are staged as mild, moderate or severe based on pain intensity, joint involvement and systemic features. Chronic gout is staged by the presence of tophi, joint damage and renal involvement.

b: Urate crystal deposition (gout) – most frequent
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout) – less common
Septic arthritis – especially in diabetics or HIV patients
Traumatic sprain or fracture of the hallux
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common causes of first MTP inflammation are:

b: Pain onset < 12 h
Erythema and warmth over the joint
Limited dorsiflexion of the hallux
sections.p: Patients describe a sudden, excruciating pain that peaks within hours, often after a heavy meal or alcohol binge. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and the toe may appear deformed (flexed). Systemic fever is uncommon unless infection is present.

b: If joint aspiration is not possible, treat as gout if clinical picture fits and infection is unlikely.
sections.p: When microscopy is unavailable, combine bedside clues with basic labs to narrow the differential.

t.a: Joint aspiration (if needle and microscope present)
t.b: Confirms crystal type; guides definitive therapy.
Leukocytosis suggests infection; normal count favours gout.
Markedly raised in septic arthritis; modest rise in gout.
Elevated (> 7 mg/dL) supports gout; normal does not rule out.

b: Fever > 38 °C, chills, or rigors
Rapidly expanding swelling with fluctuance
Immunocompromise (HIV, diabetes, chronic steroid use)
Renal impairment worsening hyperuricaemia
sections.p: Prompt recognition of infection or systemic spread prevents irreversible damage.

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) – first‑line if no renal or GI contraindication
Colchicine – useful when NSAIDs contraindicated; avoid in severe renal failure
Corticosteroid injection into the joint or short oral course – for refractory cases or when infection is excluded
Urate‑lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) – start after the acute attack resolves
sections.p: Treat the acute inflammation first, then address the underlying metabolic disturbance.

t.b: Will pain improve within 24 h? Positive response supports gout; lack of response prompts reconsideration of infection.
Rapid pain relief within 12 h indicates crystal arthritis; monitor for diarrhoea.

b: Limit purine‑rich foods, alcohol and fructose drinks
Encourage hydration (> 2 L/day) and weight control
Check serum uric acid 4–6 weeks after starting urate‑lowering therapy
Screen for renal disease and hypertension
sections.p: Educate patients on lifestyle and monitor uric acid levels to prevent recurrences.

b: Septic arthritis – distinguished by fever, high leukocytosis and purulent aspirate
Pseudogout – calcium pyrophosphate crystals are positively birefringent and rhomboid
Hallux valgus deformity – chronic deformity without acute inflammation
Normal serum uric acid during an acute attack (up to 30 % of cases)
Negative crystal analysis if fluid is scant or improperly examined
